lead: A real supply has inductance: transformer leakage, cable, alternator reactance. So when a thyristor is fired, the current cannot jump from the outgoing device to the incoming one. Both conduct for a short overlap angle µ, and during that time two supply lines are shorted together through the thyristors. Every commutation therefore loses a small slice of DC voltage, so the output falls as load current rises. The effect appears in every rectifier, and it is what limits how hard a converter can be driven in inverter mode.
prereq: You need: firing-angle operation from 2.3 and 2.4, and the inductor law v = L di/dt.

blocks.text: Every real supply has inductance. Call it Ls: the source inductance per line, in henries (H). Most of it is transformer leakage reactance; the rest is alternator reactance and wiring. An inductor obeys v = L di/dt, so its current cannot change instantly — a finite voltage moves the current at a finite rate.

items: Before commutation, one thyristor pair carries the full load current Idc.
The outgoing thyristor does not stop at once, because its line current is held by Ls. Both devices conduct for a short time.
Two supply lines are now joined through two thyristors: a two-phase short circuit, limited only by Ls and the device drops.
Current in the incoming line rises from 0 to Idc while the outgoing current falls to 0; then the outgoing device turns off and the overlap ends.

blocks.text: That interval is the overlap, and its length in electrical degrees is the overlap angle µ. In a three-phase bridge the DC output during overlap sits halfway between the two commutating phase voltages, so a slice of voltage is missing from every commutation. In a single-phase bridge all four thyristors conduct and the DC terminals are shorted for the overlap, so the output is zero there.

sections.h3: Overlap angle and the voltage lost

blocks.text: The lost area is easy to compute, because the current swings over a known range in a time fixed by the supply voltage. The average loss turns out to be a constant times the current, so it behaves like a resistor.
ΔVd = 2ωLs Idc/π (single-phase bridge)   ΔVd = 3ωLs Idc/π (three-phase bridge)
blocks.where: ω = 2πf is the angular frequency in rad/s (f in Hz); Ls is the source inductance per line in H; Idc is the steady load current in A; ΔVd is the average voltage lost from the DC output, in V.

blocks.text: cos α − cos(α + µ) = 2ωLs Idc/(√2 V) = 2ΔVd/Vd0
blocks.where: α is the firing angle; µ is the overlap angle, in the same unit as α; V is the rms supply voltage, line-to-line for a three-phase bridge and plain rms for a single-phase one; Vd0 is the ideal no-load average voltage.

items: µ grows with Idc and with Ls: more current or more reactance takes longer to transfer.
For the same current, µ is smallest when α is near 90°, because the voltage between the two commutating phases is then at its peak.

The ratio ΔVd/Idc is the commutating resistance Rc, equal to 2ωLs/π or 3ωLs/π. Some syllabi call Ls the commutating reactance and quote the drop as a per-unit reactance, which is the same number scaled by a base impedance.

blocks.text: Because ΔVd is subtracted after the cosine term, the converter behaves like an ideal rectifier in series with Rc. A smoothing choke on the DC side does not create this drop; it only keeps Idc flat so the formulas stay valid.

sections.h3: Notches, reduced range and the inverter limit

blocks.text: Because the supply is shorted during overlap, the terminal voltage collapses briefly at every commutation. On an oscilloscope the AC bus shows flat-topped notches, p of them per supply cycle for a p-pulse converter. Notches travel along the bus, disturb other loads and can cause misfiring in a neighbouring converter. Large drives are therefore fed from a dedicated transformer or fitted with a line reactor. Supply current harmonics are the subject of 2.5.

The DC side now obeys Vd = Vd0 cos α − ΔVd. The drop is present even at α = 0, so the top of the control range is lost: the converter can no longer reach Vd0, and the firing range that gives useful output is shorter. The loss is proportional to current, so regulation is poor at heavy load.

In inverter mode the overlap becomes a hard limit. The outgoing thyristor must recover its blocking ability before the voltage across it turns positive again. Recovery takes the turn-off time tq, which corresponds to a margin angle δ = ω tq, usually a few degrees.
α + µ ≤ 180° − δ,  with δ = ω tq
blocks.where: α is the firing angle; µ is the overlap angle; δ is the margin angle, in degrees; tq is the thyristor turn-off time in s; ω = 2πf in rad/s.

blocks.text: Rearranged, α_max = 180° − δ − µ. A converter running at a large current has a large µ and must use a smaller α. Push α higher and commutation failure follows: the current fails to transfer and the bridge shorts the supply.

figure.caption: Source inductance leaves the no-load voltage unchanged but makes the output droop as load current rises.

spec.aria: A flat line at 540 V and a falling line that starts at the same point and drops about 0.3 V per ampere.

examples.question: A three-phase fully controlled bridge runs from a 400 V, 50 Hz line with a source inductance of 1 mH per phase. The load current is a steady 20 A. Find the commutating reactance ωLs, the average voltage drop ΔVd, the DC output at α = 0, and the overlap angle at that point. Take Vd0 ≈ 540 V.
steps: ωLs = 314.16 × 1 × 10⁻³ = 0.3142 Ω. This is the commutating reactance.
Check Vd0 = 3√2 × 400/π = 540 V to three figures. Then Vd = 540 − 6.0 = 534.0 V.
examples.answer: ΔVd = 6.0 V, so the output at α = 0 is 534.0 V instead of 540 V, with an overlap angle of 12.1°.
examples.check:
import math
f = 50
Ls = 1e-3
Idc = 20
Vll = 400
w = 2*math.pi*f
wLs = w*Ls
dV = 3*wLs*Idc/math.pi
Vd0 = round(3*math.sqrt(2)*Vll/math.pi)
Vd = Vd0 - dV
mu = math.degrees(math.acos(1 - 2*dV/Vd0))
print(round(w, 2))
print(round(wLs, 4))
print(round(dV, 2))
print(round(Vd, 1))
print(round(mu, 1))

traps: A smoothing choke in the load does not cause overlap. It flattens Idc and so makes the overlap steady; the overlap itself comes only from inductance on the AC side.
The drop is not zero at α = 0. ΔVd is subtracted after the cosine term, so even full firing loses 6.0 V in the worked example.
Factor slip: the single-phase bridge loses 2ωLs Idc/π, the three-phase bridge 3ωLs Idc/π. Using 3 in the single-phase case is a standard error.
In the overlap formula the voltage is rms, and for a three-phase bridge it is the line voltage. Substituting a peak value or a phase voltage gives a wrong µ.
Writing the inverter condition as α + µ ≤ 180° ignores the turn-off time. The true limit is α + µ ≤ 180° − δ, and it bites earlier.

quiz.q: Define the overlap angle µ and state what causes it.
quiz.a: µ is the interval, in electrical degrees, during which the outgoing and incoming thyristors of a rectifier conduct together. It is caused by inductance on the AC supply side, which prevents the line current from changing instantly.

quiz.q: Why is the interval called a two-phase short circuit?
quiz.a: During overlap both thyristors conduct, so two supply lines are joined through them with almost no impedance between them. The only things limiting the current are the two line inductances and the device drops, exactly as in a short circuit between two phases.

quiz.q: A single-phase fully controlled bridge works from 230 V rms, 50 Hz, with Ls = 2 mH per line and Idc = 10 A. Find ΔVd.
For the bridge of the previous question, find µ at α = 0. Use Vd0 = 2√2 × 230/π = 207.1 V.
Explain why the maximum usable firing angle in inverter mode depends on the load current.
quiz.a: The outgoing thyristor needs the turn-off time tq to recover blocking, which fixes a margin angle δ = ωtq. The available angle must cover both the firing delay and the overlap: α + µ ≤ 180° − δ. A larger current means a larger µ, so α must be reduced to keep the sum within the limit; ignoring this causes commutation failure.

quiz.q: Where do the flat-topped notches in the supply voltage come from, and who suffers?
quiz.a: They come from the two-phase short circuit during overlap, which pulls the terminal voltage down for a few degrees at every commutation, p times per cycle. Other loads on the same bus see them, and a nearby converter can misfire.

beyond: Not for the exam. In HVDC transmission the converter transformer leakage is deliberately chosen as the commutating reactance, and the margin angle is controlled directly as the extinction angle γ = 180° − (α + µ). Line-commutated inverters there use γ control rather than a fixed α, because the overlap changes with DC current. The same physics appears in the input filter design of grid-tied converters and in the design of line reactors for large drives. Search for "commutation overlap", "extinction angle control HVDC" and "commutating reactance transformer design".
